  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): the random level generator recursed to ~315 KB
  and boot-looped the board, so a generated level is a copy from
  `hacks/pacman_pool.h` (24 levels, made on the host by
  `tools/pacman_levels.py` with the cells outside the round display walled
  off; the fixed level is still half of them), and the ghosts' route search is
  a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Re-run the tool after changing its mask or
  the generator's tile data. Each patch checks what it replaces. The two host
  pins that follow the game (`kBaseline`'s Pacman and the ghost-route chain)
  depend on how many `random()` values the level pick takes: re-take the chain
  with `pacman_loop_ai.c` temporarily including `pacman/pacman_ai.c`, then
  restore it and check the loop gives the same value. Its sprite sheet is
  built from `vendor/` into the build dir by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and
  never committed (3 MB as C text).
- Braid runs at 3-9 fps (0.8-2 before four rounds of work): it redraws every
  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.
- A hack can be freed before its first draw: two quick presses, or a press
  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`
  runs every hack through it. Blaster's free dereferenced NULL (it sizes a loop
  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a
  free that zeroes `NUM_ROBOTS` when `robots` is NULL.
- Deluxe is built through `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`, which includes the unmodified
  hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with overrides:
  `*transparent: False` (upstream's plane masks need colour planes, which
  `allocate_alpha_colors` reports none of) and `*doubleBuffer: False` (it was
  added when the shim drew only on the canvas, so the `XCopyArea` from its
  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).
  The wrapper then gives each throbber's GC an alpha of 26
  of 32 (upstream's translucent weight) and sends full wide circles to
  `stroke_circle`. A plain screenhack's `HackEntry` has no overrides unless a
  wrapper builds it. Its step is 45-63 ms on the device against a 32.5 ms push,
  so about 11-13 fps (14 with 64-byte cache lines); overlapping the push with
  the next step (`repaints_all`) takes it to 19 fps. Other ideas are in issue
  #54.
- Eight of the S-hack batch (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes,
  Halftone, Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole) are built through
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c` (pixmap double buffering, see `techniques.md`;
  LMorph's is `lmorph_single.c` because it needs no `HAVE_JWXYZ`). All but
  Anemotaxis and Wormhole, and Euler2D (`euler2d_single.c`), also use
  `single_precision.h` plus build-time float literals (`patch_float_literals.py`
  lists them). `single_precision.h` leaves `floor` and `ceil` on the double
  versions: Euler2D's wrapper maps them itself. After the literal pass the
  objects still showed soft-double helpers: Interaggregate's were `frand` in
  `build_field` (fixed with `single_frand.h`); Halftone's, Anemone's and
  Euler2D's are in `*_init` only, once a start. `tools/softdouble_report.py`
  lists them by function.
- To see which hacks are worth a look, flash a build with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=20`,
  log the serial port for one lap (about 40 minutes), and run
  `uv run tools/triage_hacks.py lap.log --soft` (after `pio run -e stopwatch`).
  It sorts each hack into step-bound, push-bound or paced (its own delay is the
  biggest part of the frame) and puts the soft-double calls in its object
  beside it. A hack that is step-bound with calls is a wrapper candidate;
  step-bound with none is in its drawing, not its maths (Braid, Marbling,
  Discrete, BinaryRing); paced ones gain only what the step saves, down to the
  delay (Forest 500 ms, Vines 200 ms). A wrapper that moves nothing is worth
  dropping: Bouboule built single stayed at 14.5 ms, because its cost is
  ellipse fills.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first hash that
  differs, in registry order, so repinning several hacks takes one test run
  each (about 85 s), earliest first. A hack whose frames do not change under a
  wrapper (Compass and Halftone in single precision) keeps its hash.
- Anemone's step moved between 31 and 56 ms as its arms grew and shrank, so its
  fps was 11 to 15.5 whatever one 20 s window said. Upstream opens every frame
  by filling the whole window black, which is a full frame of PSRAM writes
  (229,000 pixels a frame on the host, the strokes only about 16,000 of them),
  so `anemone_direct.c` erases only where last frame's lines were
  (`span_erase.h`, each line's box grown by its round caps): 31,000 pixels, the
  same frames, and only those rows dirty. On the board, over one 20 s window
  per lap: 30.5 fps mean (worst 20.4), step 25.2 ms. Counting pixels and
  spans written a frame on the host (a temporary counter in `hspan`) is a
  quick way to see what a hack costs before the device does. Forest waits
  500 ms between trees by design (about 2 fps, and the push is 88 rows).
- A hack that unpacks pixel values itself (Substrate and Interaggregate, in
  their `point2rgb`) assumes ordinary RGB565, but the canvas holds the bytes
  swapped. Its wrapper swaps pixels where they cross `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground`. Interaggregate shipped without this: its alpha blends
  mixed the wrong bit fields and drew rainbow noise instead of green and brown
  strokes. `test_interaggregate_blend` includes the wrapper to check one blend.
- `dump` never seeds `random()`, so a hack that picks a mode at start (Truchet,
  12 modes) shows the same one in every dump. To see others, build the hack
  alone (`probe_hacks.registry_source` and `shim_sources`) from a copy outside
  `vendor/`, with a `__attribute__((constructor))` that calls
  `srandom(atoi(getenv("SEED")))`. Cheaper: drop a temporary
  `src/hacks/zz_seed_tmp.c` with that constructor, guarded by `SEED` being set
  (`-e dump` builds every file under `src/`), run
  `SEED=n .pio/build/dump/program <index> <frames> out.raw`, and delete the
  file before running the tests. A device boot is deterministic too (Halo
  chose Ramp on five boots in a row), so a hack that picks a mode with
  `random()` always starts the same one: force another with a temporary
  `*mode:` override to measure it. Rotation reaches other modes because the
  random state differs by then.
- Hexadrop (`hexadrop_single.c`) runs at about 10 fps, under the 15 fps bar.
  Splitting its step on the device showed the maths and the edge walk cost
  0.1 ms and all the rest is canvas writes: about 860 KB of 16-bit stores
  into the PSRAM canvas a frame. Single precision, a float convex fill and
  two-pixel stores took it from 2.4 to 10.2 fps with pixel-identical frames.
  More needs a shared canvas change or rasterising in row bands.
- Halo (`halo_direct.c`, `halo_planes.h`, `halo_circles.h`) draws whole circles
  into 1-bit pixmaps and XORs two of them. Its pixmaps are packed bit planes
  (27 KB each), not colour pixmaps: 434 KB colour stand-ins made Seuss mode
  (three runs in four) 5-9 fps, because window-sized circles are millions of
  PSRAM writes, and a float circle fill alone changed nothing. A device boot
  is deterministic, so every boot picked Ramp mode and hid that: force
  `*colorMode: seuss` temporarily to measure the other mode. It overrides
  `*delay` to 10 ms (upstream asks for 100 ms), so the circles grow faster.
- StonerView's seven files are built as one unit by `stonerview_gl.c`.
  Upstream never frees its oscillator list ("how do we free this?"), so the
  wrapper frees it through the `next` links before upstream's release.
- XMatrix needs `matrix_glyphs.py` (a `pre:` script in every env), which
  converts four PNGs from `vendor/` into blobs in the build directory: they
  are never committed (1.5 MB of C text each for the large sheets). It
  registers through `xmatrix_direct.c` with `*trace: False`, which skips the
  typed "connecting" sequence it would open with (the rare "Knock, knock,
  Neo" event, `knockKnock`, is still on); `*matrixFont: small`
  gives 46 columns instead of 23. Its text modes read no text: the
  `textclient.h` stand-in never opens a source, and Xt timers never fire.
- Flurry is not ported. It draws 3,600 blended, textured quads a frame and
  needs `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`, `gluBuild2DMipmaps` and luminance-alpha
  textures, none in TinyGL here. With `gl_budget.py`'s per-vertex and
  per-pixel costs that is well under 1 fps (arithmetic, not a measurement:
  the tool cannot read a multi-file hack).
- Qix and Fireworkx both leaked on every stop, found by the restart leak test.
  Qix's `qix_free` skips each segment's `lines[i].p` array (about 48 KB per
  stop); Fireworkx below 24 bits never frees its own 565 image buffer (48 KB).
  Their wrappers (`qix_direct.c`, `fireworkx_single.c`) free the missing piece
  before calling upstream's free. LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, but
  `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0
  out.raw` names the allocating line in seconds (rebuild `-e dump` first: a
  `pio test` deletes the program).
- Starfish and Goop spent most of a frame in the shim's polygon fill (double
  maths per edge per row). `hacks/float_polygon.h` fills any even-odd polygon
  in float, optionally mixed in at an alpha in 32nds (all three colour
  channels with one multiply), and took Starfish from 8.5 to 19 fps. Goop draws
  straight onto the window (its `XCreatePixmap` is the window and the
  `XCopyArea` is skipped) and blends each blob in at the alpha upstream's jwxyz
  path uses. Its full-frame clear cost 15 ms, so `hacks/span_erase.h` erases
  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is integer now
  (see `x11shim.md`; Hexadrop has its own convex float fill). Goop is built through
  `goop_direct.c` with `HAVE_JWXYZ`; the colour-plane path needs planes the
  canvas lacks.
- A wrapper that does `#define double float` must include any header with a
  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
  pixel-identical by construction;
  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
  screen.
- Fireworkx renders at 1/`FIREWORKX_SCALE` of the width and height
  (`hacks/lowrez_put.h`: it is told the window is smaller and `XPutImage`
  draws each pixel as a square): 2.4 fps as copied, 11 at a scale of 3, 12.4 at
  4. Its glow, flash pass and 565 conversion are full-frame walks over PSRAM.
  Its header says "(GPL)" but the text is the standard permission notice.
  Everything it works in is in pixels, tuned for a window about 1024 wide: at
  152 pixels a burst filled the picture and the glow blur (energy kept, output
  doubled) saturated, so the screen was white. `tools/fireworkx_patch.py`
  (run before the float literal pass; the copy stays byte-identical) scales the
  spark speed, gravity, flash reach and velocity jitter by the render width
  over 1024, and the wrapper throws 120 sparks a shell instead of 500 and fires
  two of its four shells. 12.4-12.6 fps, with a dark background between
  bursts. The shell count cannot change (it is baked into the SSE layout), so
  the idle shells are given an endless life and no sparks.
- Loop asks for 100 ms between generations (8.7 fps with a 3.5-7 ms step); the
  registry overrides it to 50 ms. It also took `malloc(0)` returning NULL, which
  the board does and the host does not, for out of memory: square mode asks
  for a rectangle list for each of eight colour states, most empty, and it
  freed its cells and drew nothing more (a black screen at 18 fps, half the
  starts, never seen on the host). `loop_direct.c` asks for one byte, and a test
  swaps in an allocator that returns NULL for zero. Hypnowheel was dropped from
  the rotation after Rod saw it, twice (issue #73; its source, notices row and a
  `failed_ports.txt` entry stay). `hypnowheel_single_gl.c` registers it only
  with `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`, as the last entry, for measuring. A board profile
  showed about 275 ms of its 706 ms step was `double` trig in every vertex, not
  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution
  (`glshim_set_render_scale`) for 4.0 fps, still too slow for Rod.
- CWaves (`cwaves_single.c`) fills 233 columns, each a 2 by 466 rectangle, so
  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.
- A single-precision wrapper must watch for a hack that passes the address of
  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.
- Moire and Cynosure are paced by their own delays (Moire draws a 20-row chunk
  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.
- Moire2 (`moire2_direct.c`, `moire2_planes.h`, built on Halo's planes) keeps
  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
- Boing was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and plain on a small screen);
  its source, notices row and `boing_gl.c` stay, the wrapper out of the build
  filter. Its 208 scanlines are blended full-width lines and cost half its
  step: 5.0 fps with them, 8.3 without; the ball size barely matters (0.3
  saves 13 ms). HexTrail (`hextrail_single_gl.c`) draws
  every hexagon it has built, so its step climbs from about 19 ms to a ceiling
  and it restarts: use a mean over a cycle (150 s). The grid is `count * 2`
  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:
  mean 5.7 fps at upstream's 20, 9.1 at 10, 12.7 at 6 (registered,
  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Rod found 12.7 too slow once the picture filled
  (under 10 fps). Single precision gave 13.0; skipping the depth clear it
  never needs (see `gl.md`) gave 15.3, worst window 10.8. The single-precision
  wrapper adapts `get_position` and `get_rotation`: the hack passes `double`
  locals' addresses, which a float rename would write eight bytes (as Moire).
- Celtic (`celtic_single.c`, issue #37) is registered after HexTrail and takes
  a median step of 32 ms against 832 as copied (`assessment_measured.md.in`).
  The wrapper is single precision (`rint` and `floor` mapped to float: the
  header maps only some libm calls) and frees the colour table that
  `celtic_init` callocs. `tools/celtic_patch.py` does three things at build
  time. It works `t*n - floor(t*n)` out once and clamps it: in float a fused
  multiply-add made it slightly negative and the hack's `assert()` aborted
  (the 3000-frame test found it). It sizes the graph to the screen: upstream's
  margins of -600 to -900 left most of a pattern off the screen, one held 1.1
  MB on the host, and 44 of 300 random starts needed more than the board's free
  heap by a model; grid and Kennicott now use minus one edge, and the triangle
  width/2 plus two edges (its incircle is half its circumradius). And it
  scales the 0.0001 animation tick by `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE` (default 4,
  `-DCELTIC_STEP_SCALE=<n>`), which cuts the shadow look-ahead's work and a
  picture's draw calls to 100 / scale. A test bounds a pattern's host bytes
  over 150 starts. Do not shorten `*delay2`: it is a 5 s dwell on the finished
  picture upstream. It looked like a pause on black while the shim's
  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the
  picture up and the wipe follows the wait. When forcing a graph type in a
  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle
  comes out too small to fill the screen.
- A full-frame write to the PSRAM canvas costs about 25 ms whatever does it
  (memcpy, a 2 by 2 blow-up, 32-bit stores). Eruption at half size
  (`eruption_direct.c`, `lowrez_put.h`, `-DERUPTION_SCALE`) spent 26 ms of a
  39 ms step putting its image and 13 ms on the fire. `lowrez_put.h` wants
  ordinary RGB565, so Eruption's palette is swapped at `XAllocColor`.
  Interference changes every pixel each frame; telling it the window is half
  the size changes its look (its wave table is in window pixels), so it stays
  at 10.2 fps.
- Kumppa rotates its picture with `XCopyArea` from the window onto itself.
  The fine checkerboard in its trails is the hack's: copies are checked
  against a read-everything-first reference in every overlap direction.
- Piecewise (`piecewise_direct.c`) is single precision with `single_frand.h`
  (67 to 42 ms) and frees each circle's high fringe, which upstream's free
  forgets (32 blocks a stop; `leaks` named `fringe_add_intersection`).
- BinaryRing (`binaryring_single.c`) is told the display is 24 bits deep: its
  16-bit path drops every hit below one 5-bit step, so only green builds up
  and the picture stays dim. Its pixels go straight to the window as it plots
  them, and the frame's `XPutImage` into a pixmap and copy back are skipped:
  the 32-bit image was put a pixel at a time, 130 of a 240 ms step.
  `tools/binaryring_patch.py` makes `frand1`'s exponent literal a float.
- GraphStat's word list (`graphstat.h`) is copied from `vendor/` at build
  time (`firmware/vendor_data.py`); since 6.17 upstream ships the header, each
  word wrapped in `_()` for `gettext` (`x11shim/include/nls.h`). Its timing
  is in frames tuned for 30 fps, so at 10 fps a picture takes about 36 s
  instead of 12.
- EtruscanVenus (`etruscanvenus_single_gl.c`) runs on a 48 by 32 grid
  (`tools/etruscanvenus_patch.py`, upstream's 192 by 128) at half resolution;
  `-DETRUSCANVENUS_NUMU`, `-DETRUSCANVENUS_NUMV` and `-DETRUSCANVENUS_FULL`
  try others. Its modes differ: those that fill the screen are fill-bound.
  `curlicue.h` is copied from `vendor/` at build time (`vendor_data.py`).
- BlockTube was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and not much going on);
  its source, notices row, `blocktube_single_gl.c`, `gl_textures.py` and
  `blocktube_patch.py` stay, the wrapper out of the build filter. To bring
  it back, add `pre:gl_textures.py` to the three `extra_scripts` and
  `blocktube` (with its `count_the_blocks`) to `patch_float_literals.py`
  again. It drew 400 blocks
  (`tools/blocktube_patch.py`, upstream's 1,000) at half resolution with a
  10 ms delay (`"*delay: 10000"` in its registry entry, now gone);
  fog is applied per block from the modelview's z when the hack
  sets the block's colour, and a block the fog hides is not drawn. There is
  no sphere map, so each face shows the whole texture. Its texture is
  converted from `vendor/` at build time (`gl_textures.py`). It also filters
  `glEnable` of fog and texture generation, which TinyGL warns about every
  frame.
- Companion Cube and Floppy are not ported (Rod dropped both, listed in
  `failed_ports.txt`). Each Companion Cube face draws a 9,588-vertex disc:
  about 71,000 vertices a cube, three cubes by default. Floppy's model is
  26,340 vertices (about 630 KB of floats, which would not fit beside the
  current firmware in the 3 MB app partition).
- Rocks and DecayScreen were wired, looked at and dropped in the 2026-10-12
  second batch, then brought back after Rod asked for the shim to be extended.
  Rocks stamps every rock bigger than 3 pixels with `XCopyPlane` from a
  depth-1 pixmap it filled with `XFillPolygon`, and the shim drew nothing into
  a bitmap, so only the far dots showed (a 3,000-frame dump looked nearly
  black): `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` now fill bitmaps. On the board it
  runs at 17.2 fps against its own 50 ms delay, and holds 2.66 MB of PSRAM and
  all but 32 KB of the internal heap while it runs (about 180 of its 400
  bitmaps are under the 4 KB internal limit); a rotation soak that left it for
  DecayScreen read heap and PSRAM back at their idle values. DecayScreen smears
  the picture `load_image_async_simple` paints (see `x11shim.md`); without one
  it stays black. Both were host-only findings from a frame dump: look at later
  frames (3,000) as well as 400 before pinning, and read what the hack draws
  with.
- Penrose (`penrose_short_pause.c`, `tools/penrose_patch.py`) restarts after
  900 frames (about 10 s at 87 fps) instead of 3,141 once the screen is full
  and 31,415 after an error it thinks it can recover from, about six minutes
  at the board's rate with nothing moving. Upstream counts those pauses in
  frames, tuned for a fast X server, so other devices show the same stall.
- Triangle's palette is `make_smooth_colormap`, which the shim now builds the
  way upstream picks it (two to five random colours, any saturation, never
  black): its first version was always a bright rainbow, and every hack that
  asks for a smooth map changed colour with the fix (24 pinned hashes moved,
  all looked at).
- Abstractile holds about 6.1 MB of PSRAM while it runs (the free PSRAM read
  883 KB), so it leaves little for anything else: it stops and restarts clean
  in the leak test, but watch it in a rotation soak. Lisa takes 87 ms a step
  as copied (9.6 fps) and 52 ms in single precision (`lisa_single.c`, 14.3
  fps) with frames that look the same but hash differently. Worm's worms are
  one pixel wide and there are only a few on a 466 pixel screen: plain, for
  Rod to judge. XRaySwarm's host frames are white bugs and trails; whether
  that is its default look or a colour-table gap in the shim is unchecked.
- XJack (`xjack_xft.c`) types "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy" in
  Special Elite on cream paper, through the Xft stand-in. Its first host frames
  were black (it clears the window, and the shim cleared to black) and then
  half-drawn lines scrolled in from the bottom (`xjack_init` sizes the page
  before its 40 pixel margins, and xscreensaver reshapes it after): the wrapper
  sets the window background and calls `xjack_reshape`, and each has a test
  that fails without it. Upstream's `font2` of 12 is small on a 466 pixel
  panel: Rod found 16 small and 20 good, so the wrapper overrides it to 20
  (`-DXJACK_FONT_PX=<12|16|20|24>`; about 28 columns). The margins swing
  (modes 1 to 4 walk them diagonally on purpose), and the round bezel cuts the
  corners of the page. Rod has seen it on the panel. It runs at 8-16 fps, set
  by its own delay (`wait` is 46-130 ms): typing is a 0.1 ms step, scrolling
  3.9-13.8 ms with pushes of 74-241 rows. It holds no PSRAM, and a 6-minute
  capture lost 352 bytes of internal heap in three steps (see
  `assessment_measured.md.in`).
- The 2026-10-13 sixth batch (Marbling, Deco, IMSMap, MetaBalls, Munch, CCurve,
  BinaryHorizon, RotZoomer, Twang, NerveRot, Flow, Bouboule, Ant, HyperBall,
  Demon, Droste, Polyominoes, Barcode) passed every host test and then four
  of them failed on the board, none of which a host frame could show: a stack
  overflow (Polyominoes), an allocation too big for PSRAM that the host's lazy
  memory allowed (Flow), 0.6 fps (Marbling) and 1.6 fps (Droste). Flash a
  batch before calling it done. A rotation build starting at the first new
  hack (`-DSTART_HACK=\"marbling\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=30`) measures all of them
  in one 10 minute capture. Rod then took MetaBalls, Twang, Flow and Droste
  out of `g_hacks[]` (slow or margin-bound, not worth tuning). Their sources,
  wrappers and wrapper tests stay in the tree, unregistered; to bring one
  back, re-add its registry entry, expected name, pin and leak test.
- Marbling does a 5-iteration fractal noise per pixel (12 ms a step on the
  host, 1,785 ms on the board, so the host suite takes about 3 minutes
  longer). `marbling_safe.c` overrides `*gridsize` to 6 and `*iterations` to 3
  (5.4 fps, cells of 6 pixels). Upstream's `marbling_free` never frees its
  colour table (5 KB a start): the wrapper does.
- Polyominoes (`polyominoes_iterative.c`, `tools/polyominoes_patch.py`) panicked
  the board with a double exception inside `count_adjacent_blanks`: a flood
  fill that calls itself once for each blank cell, up to 360 deep in several
  puzzles, 32 bytes a level on top of the solver's frames. The build now
  replaces it with a loop over an explicit stack (frames identical to the
  recursive build). Read a puzzle hack's grid sizes, not just its frame size.
- Flow's `csegs` is `(count + 36) * ncolors * taillen` segments of 8 bytes:
  upstream's 3,000 bees and 200 colours is up to 29 MB, which the host
  provided lazily and the board refused, so the hack drew one frame and
  nothing more. The registry gives it 120 bees and 8 colours. In single
  precision its flow dies out within about 600 frames (the screen stays
  black), so it is double: 3.0-4.8 fps, about 200 ms of every step being its
  search for the next flow. A single frame at 300 frames looked right in
  both: sweep several frame counts (300, 1000, 3000) for a hack that
  restarts itself or can die out.
- CCurve's `*limit` of 200,000 segments (each a malloc and a recursion) took
  740 ms in single precision and 2.9 s in double; the wrapper caps it at 30,000.
  Its 1.4 fps is its own pacing: 0.4 s between iterations, 42 ms of work.
- Droste (`droste_small.c`) hands back a loader token on the first call and
  finishes on the next, with the pixmap's size as the rectangle, so upstream's
  own "just finished" branch runs. It loads a picture the size of the window,
  not 2.5 times it (5.4 MB as the 32-bit image `XGetImage` makes), and renders
  at half width and height through `lowrez_put.h` (630 ms became 190 ms, 4.6
  fps). `XPutPixel` is mapped to swap the pixel, since `lowrez_put.h` wants
  ordinary RGB565 and the picture holds canvas order. MetaBalls takes all but
  28 KB of the internal heap while it runs (466 row buffers of 466 bytes).
- RotZoomer and Twang (`rotzoomer_single.c`, `twang_single.c`) start their
  picture and tiles the first time `draw` finds `load_image_async_simple`
  finished. The shim finishes at once and returns NULL, so that branch never
  ran and the first draw used a NULL zoom box (exit 139). Each wrapper does
  the finishing step straight after init. Changing the shim to return a loader
  would also change Boxfit and DecayScreen, so it is Rod's call. Both are
  single precision (they call `sin` and `cos` in double for every pixel).
  RotZoomer is unpinned in `test_hacks.c`: with no grab image every frame is
  black.
- BinaryHorizon (`binaryhorizon_swapped.c`) is told the display is 24 bits
  deep. Its 16-bit path adds less than a step of a channel per hit and rounds
  its random colour walk down, so every colour drifted to black or a dim
  green (as in BinaryRing). Pixels go straight to the window, and its image
  and pixmap are one pixel big, because nothing reads them. Every 30 s it
  restarts and callocs a new pixel buffer without freeing the old one (868 KB
  on the device): the wrapper frees it and clears the window.
- Munch defaults to `*xor: True`, so `XDrawPoint` honours `GXxor` now (only
  that primitive: lines and fills still copy). `pow2.h` is our own
  `i_log2` and `to_pow2`. IMSMap needed 1-bit `XYBitmap` images, `BitmapPad`
  is 32, and Deco needed `allocate_writable_colors` and `XStoreColors` (no
  writable cells). The scorer's gap lists were wrong twice: MetaBalls'
  `XListPixmapFormats` is under `#if 0`, and Ant needed only `automata.h`, a
  file in `hacks/` that is now copied to `xs_support/`.
- NerveRot passes the address of its own `double` locals to `rgb_to_hsv`, so
  its single-precision wrapper has an adapter (as Moire's). The restart test
  under AddressSanitizer found it as a stack-buffer-overflow, but a host frame
  looked right.
- Bouboule's upstream default is a red and a blue starfield for 3D glasses,
  drawn with `GXor`, which the shim does not do. The registry overrides
  `*use3d: False` (a single colour cycling through the palette) and
  `*cycles: 0`. Twang's 3 by 3 tiles of 120 pixels leave black margins and
  clip at the round bezel; `*tileSize` is the lever.
- A wrapper that finishes an image load itself (RotZoomer, Twang, Droste) must
  also handle the hack's timed reload, which the shim finishes at once too, so
  upstream's "just finished" branch never runs again. It must also match image
  layouts: `XGetImage` gives a 32-bit image, and a hack that memcpys it into
  its own 16-bit buffer shows alternating black pixels. RotZoomer did on the
  board until the trail review caught it. Test with a flat grab image and
  assert every pixel, then change the image before a timed restart.
- A wrapper that clears state before upstream's own timed check (BinaryHorizon
  frees its buffer) reads the clock separately from upstream, and the two reads
  can straddle a second. Read it once a frame and route upstream's `time()` to
  that reading with a function-like `#define time(p)`; test it with a fake
  clock whose second read is later.
- A hack that leaks on every in-hack restart (Munch's `get_string_resource`
  result) needs a restart-loop leak test of its own: `test_hacks` restarts only
  through start and stop.
- Deluxe's `draw_star` (ten sin/cos in software `double`, #54 idea 5): a
  single-precision build gave identical frames and no device gain (step
  45.06 vs 45.12 ms, pinned, 2 rounds). Skip it; the step is the blend, the
  mask and the strokes.

</system-reminder>

"""Check that every copied third-party source has a licence notice and is
listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

Run with: uv run tools/check_notices.py
"""

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

# Copied third-party code: one directory per hack under hacks/ (top-level
# files in hacks/ are our own, e.g. the registry), plus xs_support/.
# OWN_HACK_DIRS are hack directories that hold our own code (MIT), not copies.
SUFFIXES = {".c", ".h", ".cpp"}
OWN_HACK_DIRS = frozenset({"ad_flyingtoasters"})
# Files xscreensaver ships with no header at all, covered by the package's
# licence (xscreensaver.spec: "License: BSD"); Rod approved copying them in
# issue #44. They still need a row in the notices.
PACKAGE_LICENCE_FILES = frozenset(
    {
        "xs_support/glx/buildlwo.c",
        "xs_support/glx/buildlwo.h",
        "xs_support/glx/pipeobjs.c",
        "xs_support/glx/teapot.h",
        "xs_support/glx/teapot2.h",
    }
)
HEADER_LINES = 100
NOTICE_PHRASES = (
    "permission to use, copy, modify, distribute, and sell this software",
    "permission is hereby granted, free of charge",
    "permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute this software",
    "may be copied, modified, or used as long as this copyright is retained",
)


def has_notice(text: str) -> bool:
    lines = (line.lstrip(" \t/*") for line in text.splitlines()[:HEADER_LINES])
    head = " ".join(" ".join(lines).split()).lower()
    return "copyright" in head and any(p in head for p in NOTICE_PHRASES)


def check(src_dir: Path, notices_md: Path) -> list[str]:
    notices = notices_md.read_text() if notices_md.exists() else ""
    problems = []
    candidates = sorted((src_dir / "hacks").glob("*/**/*")) + sorted(
        (src_dir / "xs_support").rglob("*")
    )
    for path in candidates:
        if path.suffix not in SUFFIXES or not path.is_file():
            continue
        rel = path.relative_to(src_dir)
        if rel.parts[0] == "hacks" and rel.parts[1] in OWN_HACK_DIRS:
            continue
        if rel.as_posix() not in PACKAGE_LICENCE_FILES and not has_notice(
            path.read_text(errors="replace")
        ):
            problems.append(f"{rel}: no licence notice in first {HEADER_LINES} lines")
        if path.name not in notices and path.stem not in notices:
            problems.append(f"{rel}: not listed in {notices_md.name}")
    # TinyGL's sources carry no per-file header, so it is checked as a
    # directory: its LICENSE beside the sources, and a mention in the notices.
    tinygl = src_dir / "tinygl"
    if tinygl.is_dir():
        if not (tinygl / "LICENSE").is_file():
            problems.append("tinygl: no LICENSE file")
        if "TinyGL" not in notices:
            problems.append(f"tinygl: not mentioned in {notices_md.name}")
    return problems


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--src", default=str(root / "firmware" / "src"))
    parser.add_argument("--notices", default=str(root / "THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md"))
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    problems = check(Path(args.src), Path(args.notices))
    for problem in problems:
        print(problem)
    return 1 if problems else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

content.content:
# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- A `failed_ports.txt` name is the scorer's: the source file's stem
  (`companion` for Companion Cube), as the assessment's rows spell it. Check
  the cross appears after regenerating.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` stops with "hypnowheel: does not compile ... 'rotator.h'
  file not found": a dropped GL port counts in the backtest and is probed
  standalone, without the GL helpers' include path. `docs/speed-backtest.md`
  was last regenerated before Hypnowheel was ported, and was not regenerated
  for the CWaves batch either. The scorer also lists calls inside code that is
  never compiled (`XCreateBitmapFromData` in Cynosure's `DO_STIPPLE` block) as
  gaps.
- `score_hacks.py` skips the names in `OWN_HACKS` (our own hacks with no
  xscreensaver source, now `ad_flyingtoasters`) and still reports any other
  registry name it cannot scan as a typo. `speed_backtest.py` runs on the host
  only the registered hacks that have a device-measured row, so a `dump` build
  without the After Dark disk (which lacks the toasters) still works.
- `probe_hacks.MEASURED_ROW` takes only a number range in the fps cell: a
  row like `| HexTrail | 10.8-50.6, mean 15.3 |` is skipped, so the assessment
  shows `-` for its step and the backtest leaves it out. Put the mean in the
  prose.
- A call to an undeclared shim function also shows up as a gap named
  `error: incompatible integer to pointer conversion ...` (the implicit `int`
  return). It is noise beside the real gap (Barcode's `utf8_to_latin1`), but it
  counts towards the band.

content.text:
Bubble3D is ported and passes on the host and in a device build, but I haven't run it on the board. It's committed on `feature/port-bubble3d` (in the worktree `.claude/worktrees/port-bubble3d`) as two commits, e51d89a and 083d237. I haven't pushed it or opened a PR.

**What it is:** Bubble3D is four vendor files, not one: `b_lockglue.c` (the entry point), `bubble3d.c`, `b_draw.c` and `b_sphere.c`, plus `bubble3d.h`. I copied them byte-identical and built each as its own `USE_GL` unit, the way upstream does. That's why there are four small `bubble3d_*gl.c` wrapper files. Without the first one the hack won't register, but I didn't try building them as one unit.

**One fix, in the wrapper only:** upstream's `init()` builds a sphere and throws it away on every start. That leaked about 1,280 triangles per restart, and the restart leak test caught it. The wrapper makes that call return NULL, since nothing uses the result.

**What I checked** (reported separately, as per the project rules):
- **Compiles:** the host dump build and the device build (`-e stopwatch`) both succeed, at 49.4% of flash.
- **Host tests pass:** the full native suite passes (812 of 812) and so do the tool tests (593, with 3 skipped). `check_notices.py` passes and `cmp` shows all five files identical to `vendor/`.
- **Red-then-green:** the registry and leak tests failed before the port and pass after.
- **Frames:** I looked at host frames at 200 and 1000 steps. You get lit, wobbling bubbles rising on black, and the frame hash is pinned.
- **Not done:** it hasn't run on the device. The bubbles look opaque rather than see-through, and each shows a dark wedge inside it; I haven't investigated either.

**Decisions and things to know:**
- **Licence:** only `bubble3d.c` has a permission notice. You chose to list the other four files under the same xlock notice, so I did that and added them to `PACKAGE_LICENCE_FILES` in `tools/check_notices.py`.
- **Scorer:** it knew this hack as `b_lockglue`, so it rejected `bubble3d` as a typo. I added a one-line name map in `tools/score_hacks.py`, with a test, and regenerated the assessment.
- **Pre-commit:** the `ty` hook can't find `ty` in the shared `.venv`, so I committed with `SKIP=ty`. I ran `uvx ty check --python .venv` instead, and it passes.
- **Speed worry:** `glb_bubble_draw` does 5 software-`double` `cos` calls per vertex per bubble, roughly 25,000 a frame at the default 8 bubbles. I expect that to be slow on the S3, but I have no numbers yet. The hack also uses `GL_AUTO_NORMAL`, which TinyGL warns about and ignores; the bubbles supply their own normals, so I don't think it matters.
- **Resource warnings:** the dump prints "no default for resource" for `ncolors`, `cycles` and `count`. They look harmless, so I left them.

**Decision for you:** may I flash it, so I can measure fps and heap as copied? If it's slow, my plan is a single-precision wrapper, as for HexTrail. I haven't started that.

Still to do before a PR: measure on the device, add the numbers to `tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, and then run `entire trail create` for the draft PR.

# Flashing and measuring on the device

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build. Unescaped quotes fail
  with "error: 'truchet' was not declared in this scope".
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod" over
  "Begbie"; `\n` starts a new line). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  `-DQR_URL=\"https://example.com\"` sets the QR overlay's target (default the
  LinkedIn profile). Check it reached the binary with
  `strings -a .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c 'example.com'`.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- Serial log: read `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 for N seconds into a file
  (a pyserial script run with `.venv/bin/python -I`). Run it in the background
  with absolute paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= sync= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack,
  the push, the wait for the panel's TE edge before a synced push (only
  Unknown Pleasures; not counted in `push=`) and the wait; mean canvas rows
  sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
  Set `dtr` and `rts` to False on an unopened `serial.Serial()` before
  `open()`: a reopen loop without that once parked the chip in its bootloader
  (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen). Recover, or reset just
  before a capture to log from boot (a hack's `fprintf(stderr)` reaches the
  log), with `.venv/bin/python .platformio/packages/tool-esptoolpy/esptool.py
  --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 --after hard_reset read_mac`.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `ad-flyingtoasters` force flags (add to `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS`):
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_ART=0|1` (0 is 1-bit, 1 is colour) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_DONENESS=0|1|2` (light, medium, dark) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1|2` (2 is the default, with 6 flyers; 1 is the
  original size, with 10); a number outside those is an `#error`. It logs
  `ad-flyingtoasters: <art>, doneness=<level>` to stderr at start.
- To see where a GL hack's frame goes, add `-DGL_PROFILE`: a `glprof` line
  follows each `run` line with time per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill). Time left
  over is the hack's own code. To compare builds, `.venv/bin/python -I
  tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 --out <dir>
  "a=-DGL_PROFILE" "b=-DGL_PROFILE -DFOO"` builds each variant pinned, flashes
  them in turn and tabulates the windows. It flashes: run it only with Rod's
  go-ahead. It builds each hack's variants from the working tree when that
  hack's turn starts, so leave `src/` and `tools/tinygl_patch.py` alone until
  the last hack has built. It compares flag variants of one tree: to A/B a
  change, put it behind a temporary `-D` switch (as `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` does).
  It takes one `--hack` per run: loop several from a scratchpad script run
  with `run_in_background`, and `touch` a done file at the end.
- `-DDCACHE_LINE32` keeps the SDK's 32-byte data-cache lines for every hack
  (the default is 64 bytes, see `device-display.md`), so it is the A side of an
  `ab_flash` comparison. `-DPSRAM_BENCH` boots into `diag/psram_bench.h`
  instead of the runner and prints cost per cache miss, sequential rates and a
  working-set sweep; `-DPSRAM_BENCH_VARIANT=0..3` picks the line size and
  prefetch setting.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- Another session may be using the board. Before flashing, run `lsof
  /dev/cu.usbmodem112401`: a "multiple access on port" upload error was
  another session's serial capture, and esptool's connect resets the board
  under it. Ask Rod before flashing over someone else's run.
- PlatformIO cleans the build directory, image and all, when
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` changes: an `-t nobuild -t upload` with other flags
  finds no `firmware.bin`. To keep several images, give each its own
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_DIR` (the build scripts all use `$BUILD_DIR`).
- Read `push=` from a hack's second 5 s window on: the name overlay is stamped
  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- `heap=` and `psram=` are the reading at the end of a window, not a minimum:
  a hack with a long pause and nothing held in it (Celtic's 5 s `*delay2`)
  reads idle in every window. Sample while it works, or read `rotate ->`.
- Report a hack's lowest `fps=` window as well as its mean. HexTrail's step
  grows over a 65 s cycle: mean 15.3, worst window 10.8, and Rod saw an earlier
  build sag under 10 fps before the rotation moved on. Capture a full cycle and
  say which build the board holds when you stop.
- A boot is deterministic (same hack, layout and windows), so to compare two
  builds flash them alternately and compare window by window; one reading in
  three captures was an unexplained outlier, so never trust a single pair.
- Leak-testing with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5`: internal heap falls about 26 KB
  during the first lap and then stays flat. Compare lap 2 with lap 3, not
  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.
- To prove a device-only path the host cannot run (the ROM's `tinfl`), add a
  temporary `#ifdef` block after `printStats("boot")` in `main.cpp` that logs
  a checksum, compare it with one computed in Python, then `git checkout
  firmware/src/main.cpp` before pushing.

---
name: stopwatch-serial-port-discovery
description: How to find the StopWatch's serial port when /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 is missing (the name changes with the USB port)
metadata:
  type: reference
---

The StopWatch (ESP32-S3, native USB) shows up as "USB JTAG/serial debug unit",
vendor Espressif (idVendor 12346 = 0x303a, idProduct 4097 = 0x1001). macOS names
the port from the USB location, so a different physical port or cable changes
`/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` (the name in AGENTS.md) to something else
(`/dev/cu.usbmodem101` on 2026-10-14).

Read-only lookup, no contact with the board:

```text
ioreg -p IOUSB -l -w0 | grep -E "\+-o|idVendor|idProduct|USB Product Name|USB Serial Number"
ioreg -r -c IOSerialBSDClient -l | grep IOCalloutDevice
```

Match the Espressif entry, then take the `usbmodem` callout device. The USB
serial number is the board's MAC (`28:84:85:43:B2:70` for Rod's board).

**Why:** the fixed port in AGENTS.md went stale and flashing to a wrong port is
hard to undo. Rod confirmed this lookup as the way to find it.

**How to apply:** if `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` is missing, run the lookup, check
the MAC against this one, then flash with `--upload-port <port>` rather than
editing `platformio.ini`. Still ask Rod before each flash, and `lsof` the port
first. A flash with an overridden port was blocked by the auto-mode classifier
once, so expect to hand Rod the command to run with `!`.

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

## Mental Model

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[List Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Code Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Text Block]
[EOF]
```

Every block transition = blank line required.

## Quick Patterns

**List:**

```markdown
text

- item

text
```

**Heading:**

```markdown
text

## Head

text
```

**Code:**

````markdown
text

```lang
code
```

text
````

**Nested:**

```markdown
- parent
  - child
- parent
```

**Ordered:**

```markdown
text

1. item
1. item

text
```

**Table:**

```markdown
text

| Header | Header |
| --- | --- |
| Cell | Cell |

text
```

## Common Languages

**Programming:** `python` `javascript` `java` `c` `cpp` `go` `rust` `ruby`
`php` `swift` `kotlin` `typescript`

**Shell:** `bash` `sh` `powershell` `cmd` `zsh`

**Markup:** `html` `css` `xml` `json` `yaml` `toml` `markdown`

**Database:** `sql` `postgresql` `mysql`

**Other:** `text` `diff` `log`

## Validation

```bash
markdownlint filename.md
```

Goal: Zero errors/warnings.

## Additional Resources

See bundled references:

- `references/complete-rules.md` - Full rule catalog
- `references/edge-cases.md` - Platform quirks
- `references/examples.md` - Detailed examples

## Remember

Most common: Missing blank lines around lists/headings/code.

**Two trailing spaces:** Intentional line breaks. Do NOT remove.

When in doubt:

1. Add blank lines before/after blocks
2. Use `-` for lists
3. Use `#` for headings
4. Specify code language
5. Increment headings by one
6. Use regular spaces only
7. Two trailing spaces = line break

---
name: device-run
description: Use when flashing the StopWatch, pinning a hack or setting build flags (START_HACK, ROTATE_SECONDS, BADGE_NAME, QR_URL, toaster flags, GL_PROFILE), capturing the serial log, A/B testing builds with ab_flash.py, or reading fps, push, heap and psram on the device.
---

# Flashing and measuring on the device

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build. Unescaped quotes fail
  with "error: 'truchet' was not declared in this scope".
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod" over
  "Begbie"; `\n` starts a new line). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  `-DQR_URL=\"https://example.com\"` sets the QR overlay's target (default the
  LinkedIn profile). Check it reached the binary with
  `strings -a .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c 'example.com'`.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- Serial log: read `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 for N seconds into a file
  (a pyserial script run with `.venv/bin/python -I`). Run it in the background
  with absolute paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= sync= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack,
  the push, the wait for the panel's TE edge before a synced push (only
  Unknown Pleasures; not counted in `push=`) and the wait; mean canvas rows
  sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
  Set `dtr` and `rts` to False on an unopened `serial.Serial()` before
  `open()`: a reopen loop without that once parked the chip in its bootloader
  (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen). Recover, or reset just
  before a capture to log from boot (a hack's `fprintf(stderr)` reaches the
  log), with `.venv/bin/python .platformio/packages/tool-esptoolpy/esptool.py
  --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 --after hard_reset read_mac`.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `ad-flyingtoasters` force flags (add to `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS`):
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_ART=0|1` (0 is 1-bit, 1 is colour) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_DONENESS=0|1|2` (light, medium, dark) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1|2` (2 is the default, with 6 flyers; 1 is the
  original size, with 10); a number outside those is an `#error`. It logs
  `ad-flyingtoasters: <art>, doneness=<level>` to stderr at start.
- To see where a GL hack's frame goes, add `-DGL_PROFILE`: a `glprof` line
  follows each `run` line with time per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill). Time left
  over is the hack's own code. To compare builds, `.venv/bin/python -I
  tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 --out <dir>
  "a=-DGL_PROFILE" "b=-DGL_PROFILE -DFOO"` builds each variant pinned, flashes
  them in turn and tabulates the windows. It flashes: run it only with Rod's
  go-ahead. It builds each hack's variants from the working tree when that
  hack's turn starts, so leave `src/` and `tools/tinygl_patch.py` alone until
  the last hack has built. It compares flag variants of one tree: to A/B a
  change, put it behind a temporary `-D` switch (as `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` does).
  It takes one `--hack` per run: loop several from a scratchpad script run
  with `run_in_background`, and `touch` a done file at the end.
- `-DDCACHE_LINE32` keeps the SDK's 32-byte data-cache lines for every hack
  (the default is 64 bytes, see `device-display.md`), so it is the A side of an
  `ab_flash` comparison. `-DPSRAM_BENCH` boots into `diag/psram_bench.h`
  instead of the runner and prints cost per cache miss, sequential rates and a
  working-set sweep; `-DPSRAM_BENCH_VARIANT=0..3` picks the line size and
  prefetch setting.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- Another session may be using the board. Before flashing, run `lsof
  /dev/cu.usbmodem112401`: a "multiple access on port" upload error was
  another session's serial capture, and esptool's connect resets the board
  under it. Ask Rod before flashing over someone else's run.
- PlatformIO cleans the build directory, image and all, when
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` changes: an `-t nobuild -t upload` with other flags
  finds no `firmware.bin`. To keep several images, give each its own
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_DIR` (the build scripts all use `$BUILD_DIR`).
- Read `push=` from a hack's second 5 s window on: the name overlay is stamped
  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- `heap=` and `psram=` are the reading at the end of a window, not a minimum:
  a hack with a long pause and nothing held in it (Celtic's 5 s `*delay2`)
  reads idle in every window. Sample while it works, or read `rotate ->`.
- Report a hack's lowest `fps=` window as well as its mean. HexTrail's step
  grows over a 65 s cycle: mean 15.3, worst window 10.8, and Rod saw an earlier
  build sag under 10 fps before the rotation moved on. Capture a full cycle and
  say which build the board holds when you stop.
- A boot is deterministic (same hack, layout and windows), so to compare two
  builds flash them alternately and compare window by window; one reading in
  three captures was an unexplained outlier, so never trust a single pair.
- Leak-testing with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5`: internal heap falls about 26 KB
  during the first lap and then stays flat. Compare lap 2 with lap 3, not
  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.
- To prove a device-only path the host cannot run (the ROM's `tinfl`), add a
  temporary `#ifdef` block after `printStats("boot")` in `main.cpp` that logs
  a checksum, compare it with one computed in Python, then `git checkout
  firmware/src/main.cpp` before pushing.

content.text:
Bubble3D runs on the board without crashing, but it's slow: about 3.8 fps at first, sagging to 2.6 fps as more bubbles fill in. That's well under the 10 fps bar.

**Flash:** it went through on `/dev/cu.usbmodem101` and all four images report "Hash of data verified". The board now holds a Bubble3D-pinned build with rotation off, which is not the conference firmware. Nothing was written near `ffat`.

**Serial capture** (75 s, 14 windows of `run Bubble3D`):

| Window | fps | step | push | heap free | PSRAM free |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| first (1 bubble) | 5.2 | 188 ms | 5.0 ms | 256,792 | 5.73 MB |
| second to fifth | 3.4–3.8 | 254–299 ms | 0.2–0.6 ms | 256,560 | 5.73 MB |
| last (around 8 bubbles) | 2.6 | 390 ms | 5.4 ms | 256,560 | 5.73 MB |

- **Cause:** the step grows with the number of bubbles, so the time is in drawing and not in the push. The push stays under 6 ms, so the board isn't waiting on the panel.
- **Memory:** heap and PSRAM are flat after the first window, so there's no visible leak here. A leak would need a rotation lap to show.
- **Warnings:** the log shows the same resource warnings and the `GL_AUTO_NORMAL` warning as on the host.
- **Not yet measured:** the lowest window is 2.6 fps, and I haven't seen it past about 75 s, so the long-run mean may be a little lower.

**What I think the cost is:**
- The `glb_bubble_draw` `cos` calls in software `double`, about 25,000 a frame.
- About 1,280 lit triangles per bubble with three lights.

I haven't split the step to see which dominates. The way to find out is a `-DGL_PROFILE` flash, which also needs your go-ahead.

**Two things I'd like from you:**
- **Please look at the screen:** do the bubbles look right, and is the colour sensible? Host frames can't show a byte swap. The host showed opaque bubbles with a dark wedge inside each, so check whether that wedge is there.
- **Approval for another flash:** approval for the last one doesn't extend. I'd flash a `GL_PROFILE` build, to split the step before changing anything. If it confirms the maths, I'd write a single-precision wrapper (as for HexTrail). Cutting `subdivision_depth` from 3 to 2 would quarter the triangles, but that's a look change, so I'd ask you first. I'd also drop Bubble3D if it still can't get near 10 fps.

content.content:
## Single precision

When: a hot loop does `double` maths or calls `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt` or `pow`.
The ESP32-S3 has a single-precision FPU only, so double runs in software.

- Find the hot loop first and count the calls. Substrate makes four `sin` calls
  per sand grain, with 64 grains a crack and up to 100 cracks: about 25,000
  software `sin`s a frame. Its step grew from 5 ms to 121 ms as the picture
  filled.
- Wrapper `hacks/<name>_single.c`: include the framework headers first, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h`, then the unmodified hack. Exclude the original in
  `build_src_filter` of all three environments.
- `M_PI` is a double literal, so the angle arithmetic stays double: put
  `#undef M_PI` and a float definition after the header. Literals such as
  `0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
  and now go through it too, with `single_constants.h` (`MAXRAND`, `M_PI`) and
  `single_frand.h`. Run `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` on the
  wrapper's object after `pio run -e stopwatch`: any count in a per-frame
  function means a literal, macro or `double` struct field the rename missed
  (`x11shim.md` has the four that did). A trig argument that is a big whole
  number is a fifth: look at a frame before trusting the float build.
- A plain single-precision wrapper is cheap to try: include
  `single_precision.h`, `single_constants.h` and `<name>_floatlit.c`, exclude
  the original in the three `build_src_filter` lines and list the name in
  `patch_float_literals.py`. Measure it on the board and drop it if it moves
  nothing. On the board, step before to after: Hopalong 7-20 to 3.4 ms,
  WhirlWindWarp 6-26 to 3.8 ms, BinaryHorizon 95.8 to 31.8 ms, Barcode 77.1 to
  56.1 ms (frames byte-identical), XSpirograph 44.2 to 10.9 ms, Vines 182 to
  10.3 ms; Bouboule stayed at 14.5 ms.
- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
  literals first.
- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and

/* Builds hextrail.c with USE_GL set for this file only (see hacks/gears_gl.c),
 * in single precision, and with its decimal literals made floats at build
 * time (tools/float_literals.py). The hack walks every hexagon each frame and
 * does its colour, size and corner maths in `double`, which the ESP32-S3's
 * FPU does in software.
 *
 * It passes the addresses of `double` locals to get_position and
 * get_rotation, which take `double *`: as floats they would be written eight
 * bytes (see moire_single.c). The adapters come before single_precision.h, so
 * their `double` is the real one.
 *
 * Each hexagon's `pos` and every corner are `XYZ`, which normals.h declares
 * with `double` fields before single_precision.h can rename them, so every
 * vertex (`h->pos.x + corners[j].x * size1`) was a software double add and
 * multiply. The hack only stores XYZ (it never calls calc_normal), so
 * normals.h sees its own name for the double struct and the hack gets a float
 * one. */
#define USE_GL
#include <math.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

#include "xlockmore.h"
#include "colors.h"
#define XYZ glx_double_xyz
#include "normals.h"
#undef XYZ
#include "rotator.h"
#include "gltrackball.h"

static void hextrail_get_position(rotator *rot, float *x, float *y, float *z,
                                  Bool update_p) {
  double dx, dy, dz;
  get_position(rot, &dx, &dy, &dz, update_p);
  *x = (float)dx;
  *y = (float)dy;
  *z = (float)dz;
}

/* Builds hextrail.c with USE_GL set for this file only (see hacks/gears_gl.c),
 * in single precision, and with its decimal literals made floats at build
 * time (tools/float_literals.py). The hack walks every hexagon each frame and
 * does its colour, size and corner maths in `double`, which the ESP32-S3's
 * FPU does in software.
 *
 * It passes the addresses of `double` locals to get_position and
 * get_rotation, which take `double *`: as floats they would be written eight
 * bytes (see moire_single.c). The adapters come before single_precision.h, so
 * their `double` is the real one.
 *
 * Each hexagon's `pos` and every corner are `XYZ`, which normals.h declares
 * with `double` fields before single_precision.h can rename them, so every
 * vertex (`h->pos.x + corners[j].x * size1`) was a software double add and
 * multiply. The hack only stores XYZ (it never calls calc_normal), so
 * normals.h sees its own name for the double struct and the hack gets a float
 * one. */
#define USE_GL
#include <math.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

#include "xlockmore.h"
#include "colors.h"
#define XYZ glx_double_xyz
#include "normals.h"
#undef XYZ
#include "rotator.h"
#include "gltrackball.h"

static void hextrail_get_position(rotator *rot, float *x, float *y, float *z,
                                  Bool update_p) {
  double dx, dy, dz;
  get_position(rot, &dx, &dy, &dz, update_p);
  *x = (float)dx;
  *y = (float)dy;
  *z = (float)dz;
}

content.text:
The `GL_PROFILE` flash worked, and I've now written and committed a single-precision wrapper. That wrapper hasn't been flashed. Flashing it needs your go-ahead, because approval for earlier flashes doesn't carry over.

**Profile from the board.** The board currently holds the `GL_PROFILE` build of the double version. At about 8 bubbles:

| Part of the step | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Whole step | 300–390 ms |
| `vertex` (TinyGL's per-vertex work, including triangles and fill) | 86–156 ms |
| Hack's own code outside GL | about 220 ms |

- **What the 220 ms is:** one software-`double` `cos` per nudge axis per vertex, roughly 25,000 a frame. That fits what the soft-double report showed.
- **Why it sags:** the step grows from 300 ms to 390 ms as bubbles fill the screen. That growth is in the GL part: triangle time rises from 23 ms to 93 ms, and fill from 6 ms to 28 ms. Larger bubbles mean more pixels to fill.
- **Vertices:** all 30,720 vertices go through TinyGL every frame, in every window.

**The fix (3f134e9).** `bubble3d.c` is now built through `bubble3d_bubble_gl.c` with `single_precision.h`, `single_constants.h` and a build-time float-literal pass. `bubble3d` is listed in `patch_float_literals.py`, which also rewrites the hack's local `#include` so the generated copy finds its header.
- **Hack still copied:** the vendored files are untouched.
- **Frames:** host frames are byte-identical to the double build at 200 and 1000 steps, so the pinned hash didn't move.
- **Soft double:** the `bubble3d.c` object has 0 soft-double calls, and `test_hacks` passes (119 of 119).
- **Predicted effect:** removing about 220 ms should leave roughly 100–170 ms, or about 6–9 fps. That's my arithmetic, not a measurement.

**Next flash, if you approve.** I'd flash the pinned build without `GL_PROFILE`, so profiling doesn't skew the timing, and capture about 75 s again. The step will probably still grow as bubbles fill the screen, so I'd read the lowest window as well as the mean.

If it lands near 10 fps, I'd stop there. If it doesn't, the remaining lever is the triangle count and the fill. `subdivision_depth` 3 → 2 quarters the triangles, but it makes the bubbles look more faceted, so I'd ask you before changing it.

Can I flash it?

content.text:
The single-precision build is a real gain, but it's still too slow. Even the best window is only about 10 fps, and it settles around 4–5 fps.

The flash went through (4 hashes verified), and I captured 100 s from `/dev/cu.usbmodem101`:

| Window | fps | step | push |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| first (1 bubble) | 10.0 | 88 ms | 4.6 ms |
| third (about 2 bubbles) | 7.2 | 130 ms | 0.6 ms |
| fifth | 5.2 | 187 ms | 3.3 ms |
| settled, about 8 bubbles | 4.6–4.8 | 199–209 ms | 5–7 ms |
| last | 4.0–4.2 | 232–241 ms | 8–14 ms |

- **Against the double build:** the first window went from 5.2 fps (188 ms) to 10.0 fps (88 ms). At full bubbles the step went from about 390 ms to about 205 ms, so the maths fix took roughly half the cost off. The worst window is 4.0 fps, against 2.6 before.
- **Worst case:** about 4.0 fps in the final windows, and it's still sagging there.
- **Push:** it climbs to 13.7 ms and the wait drops to 0, with `rows=466` meaning every frame pushes the whole screen. The bubbles now cover most of it. The step is still the main cost.
- **Memory:** heap and PSRAM are flat apart from small steps late on (PSRAM free 5.73 MB → 5.71 MB). I haven't tracked down what causes those, and a rotation lap would show whether they accumulate.

The remaining cost is TinyGL, not the maths. It does 30,720 vertices and about 10,000 triangles a frame, each lit by three lights, and the fill grows as the bubbles grow.

**Options, cheapest first. Each needs another flash, so I'd ask before each:**
1. **`subdivision_depth` 3 → 2** quarters the triangles and vertices. It's a one-line override from the wrapper and the vendor file stays untouched. Bubbles would look slightly more faceted, and on a 466 px round screen that may be fine. I'd guess 8–10 fps, but I haven't measured it.
2. **Fewer bubbles** (`max_bubbles` 8 → 4) cuts the fill and vertex counts, but makes the screen emptier.
3. **Render at half resolution** (`glshim_set_render_scale`, as EtruscanVenus does) cuts fill by 4×, but makes edges softer.
4. **Drop it**, as you did with Boing and BlockTube, if none of that looks good enough. The source, notices and wrappers would stay in the tree.

My suggestion is option 1 first, then decide by eye. It's a look change, so it's your call. Which would you like?

The board holds the pinned Bubble3D single-precision build with rotation off. Two commits are not pushed: 3f134e9, and c9da3b8 for the port lookup.

/* Builds the unmodified Bubble3D sources with USE_GL set for each file alone, as
 * upstream builds them, so no other hack sees a GL build. See hacks/gears_gl.c.
 *
 * Upstream's own GLB_SLOW_GL switch takes the bubble sphere from 3 subdivisions
 * (1,280 triangles) to 2 (320). Depth 3 ran at 4-5 fps on the board, with 30,720
 * vertices a frame through TinyGL.
 *
 * b_lockglue.c's init() builds a sphere and drops the result (the sphere that
 * draws is b_draw.c's own), leaking it on every start. Nothing reads that
 * value, so here the call returns NULL. */
#define USE_GL
#include "bubble3d/bubble3d.h"

#undef GLB_SLOW_GL
#define GLB_SLOW_GL 1
#define glb_sphere_init() NULL
#include "bubble3d/b_lockglue.c"

content.text:
Depth 2 is done and `feature/port-bubble3d` is pushed to origin. I haven't flashed depth 2, so I don't have a device speed for it yet.

**The change (433c5ae):** `bubble3d_gl.c` now turns on upstream's own `GLB_SLOW_GL` switch, which takes the bubble sphere from 3 subdivisions (1,280 triangles) to 2 (320). It's a one-line override and the vendor files are untouched.
- **Look:** the host frame at 200 steps looks close to the depth-3 one, with the same layout and colours. The two differ by 10,223 bytes, so the change took effect.
- **Tests:** I repinned the Bubble3D hash to `0x7512dd38b81f385b` after looking at the frame, and `test_hacks` passes (119 of 119). That was the only test run since the change. The earlier full native suite and tool tests predate the depth change.

**Push:** the branch has five commits on it. The new branch carries c9da3b8, the port lookup in the `device-run` skill, which is separate from Bubble3D, so tell me if you'd rather it went in its own PR. Pushing also sent 4 Entire checkpoint refs.

**Not done yet:**
- **No PR:** you didn't ask for one, and I'd open it as a draft with `entire trail create` once the numbers are in.
- **Not on the board:** it still holds the previous single-precision depth-3 build. Measuring depth 2 needs one more flash, which I'd do with your go-ahead.
- **No assessment row:** once I have the numbers I'd add Bubble3D's measured row to `tools/assessment_measured.md.in`.
- **Needs your eye:** the dark wedge inside each bubble is still there, and I haven't investigated it.

Shall I flash depth 2 and measure?
